docs.title: Cap Collective — School Implementation Kit
docs.text:
"The distance between an idea and its impact is the bridge we build today."

Welcome to the Cap Collective documentation. This is a complete, open-source K-12 circular economy program where students collect HDPE bottle caps, process them into flakes, and manufacture valuable products — all while learning STEM, entrepreneurship, and environmental stewardship.

docs.title: 🎯 What Is Cap Collective?
docs.text:
Cap Collective is a student-led circular recycling program that captures discarded plastic bottle caps and transforms them into useful products (coasters, keychains, organizers, tiles) while funding school gardens and grants.

The Problem: Only ~3% of bottle caps are recycled globally. They're too small for industrial sorting machines — they fall through the cracks.

The Solution: Source separation at school + micro-manufacturing = high-value products + measurable impact + standards-aligned curriculum.

docs.title: 32. Digital Products & Online Store
docs.text: Purpose: Sell student-made products online (Eco-Store), publish digital goods (lesson plan packs, certificates, the kit itself), and turn revenue into the program's operating budget.

docs.title: Checkout flow
docs.text:
1. Student adds items (browser-side cart in localStorage).
  2. "Pay online" → serverless checkout creates a secure Stripe payment link.
  3. "Order for pickup" → order summary is emailed to the Eco-Store manager (student-run).
  4. Student production crew builds the order, checks QC (doc 10), and ships or hands over.

docs.title: Pricing rules
docs.text:
• Price ≥ 2× material cost + a small labor credit per student production hour.
  • Proceeds split: 40% materials & repairs, 40% garden/community fund, 20% event fund.
  • Never discount below material cost even for friends (protects the learning economy).

docs.title: 2. Digital Products (recurring revenue)
docs.text:
• Lesson pack re-licensing: other schools pay a small fee to use the curriculum with a licensed copy (buy once, reuse year after year).
  • Certificate print packs: schools order printable certification templates.
  • Pro receipts/impact reports for sponsors (doc 23) — a paid tier with extra fidelity.

Keep prices humble; the goal is sustainability, not profit.

docs.title: 3. Processing & Compliance
docs.text:
• Online card payments: use Stripe, with a school/org bank account behind it.
  • Wait until v2 to take international orders — ship domestic first.
  • Handle VAT/tax with your finance contact (doc 13); student re-issue receipts only via the template.
  • All products must carry a care label: "Recycled HDPE/PP; keep under 60°C — do not microwave."

docs.title: 4. Inventory Batching
docs.text:
Produce in batches, not per-order:

Batch Target Trigger Keychains & coasters 40 units Every 2 weeks Phone stands / organizers 10 units Every month Plant pots / art tiles 8 units Monthly or on demand

Unify batches with the Command Center sheet so QC and sales always have stock numbers.

docs.title: 5. Success Metrics (semester)
docs.text:
• $500+ revenue from store + digital products.
  • ≥ 60% of product inventory sold (avoid dead stock).
  • Average 3-day turnaround from order to pickup.
  • Every order linked to a logged production batch (measured impact).

docs.text: Covers pricing, point-of-sale, inventory, events, online sales, and money handling.

docs.title: PART 1: STORE CONCEPT & POLICY
docs.text:
What it is: A student-run pop-up shop selling recycled-cap products (coasters, organizers, keychains, keychains, pots). Revenue funds the garden and materials.

Two operating models — pick one: | Model | Best for | Notes | |-------|----------|-------| | Pop-up shop | Most schools | Open during lunch/events only; low overhead | | Online store | Larger programs | Etsy/Square/Shopify; needs adult account-holder |

Policy check: Confirm with the business office whether the school can accept revenue, or whether sales must route through a booster/PTA 501(c)(3). Never run sales through a personal account.

docs.title: The Formula
docs.text:
PRICE = (MATERIAL + OVERHEAD + LABOR) × MARKUP

Material: caps (free) + color, hardware, packaging
Overhead: electricity, wear, consumables (allocate ~10%)
Labor: student time × $0 (educational) OR small stipend
Markup: 2.5-3× for retail

Example: weekly sales 6, lead time 1 week, safety 4 → reorder at ≤10

docs.title: 1. PROJECT TITLE
docs.text: Cap Collective: A Student-Led Circular Economy & STEM Program at [School Name]

docs.title: 2. PROJECT SUMMARY (150 words)
docs.text:
Cap Collective is a student-run circular economy program that diverts HDPE bottle cap waste from landfill while teaching STEM, entrepreneurship, and environmental stewardship. Students collect caps on campus, process them through a 5-step cycle (Collect → Clean → Shred → Melt → Refine), and manufacture saleable products such as coasters, desk organizers, and plant pots. All revenue funds the school garden and program sustainability.

In Year 1, [School Name] will engage [50-300] students, divert [10,000+] caps ([35+] kg) from landfill, avoid [65+] kg CO₂e, and generate [$500+] in product revenue — with every student certified in safe machine operation. The program is curriculum-aligned, replicable, and open-source, positioning [School Name] as a regional leader in sustainability education.

docs.title: 3. STATEMENT OF NEED (250 words)
docs.text:
The problem: Globally, only 3% of bottle caps are recycled. Bottle caps are among the top five deadliest marine debris items, frequently ingested by wildlife because of their small size and bright colors. Even where recycling exists, caps are too small for industrial sorting machinery and fall through the cracks — ending up in landfill or oceans.

The local gap: [School Name] currently sends approximately [__] kg of mixed plastic waste to general waste each term. Caps are mixed with bottles, contaminating recycling streams and losing value. Students witness this waste daily but lack a system to act — a gap between intent and impact.

Why us: Our school is a high-consumption hub with [] students. A single lunch hour generates [] plastic bottles. We have the space, the staff commitment, and the student interest to convert this liability into an asset. What we lack is seed funding for equipment and safety infrastructure — the exact barrier this grant removes.

Why now: [School Name] is expanding its STEM and sustainability curriculum. Cap Collective offers a ready-made, standards-aligned anchor unit that turns a school-wide environmental problem into a hands-on learning and revenue opportunity.

docs.title: 4. PROGRAM DESIGN (300 words)
docs.text:
Phase 1 — Launch (Weeks 1-2): Secure administrative approval and a ventilated workspace; procure equipment; recruit program lead and student team; sign safety MOU.

Phase 2 — Collect (Weeks 3-4): Map high-traffic collection zones; build and deploy [5+] laser-cut collection boxes with IR sensors; launch during school assembly; complete student safety certification.

Phase 3 — Process (Weeks 5-8): Run weekly cycles — collect, wash, shred, press, finish. Track all data in the Command Center dashboard. Produce first product batch.

Phase 4 — Product (Weeks 9-12): Run a design sprint; design molds in Fusion 360; produce three product lines; implement student-led quality control.

Phase 5 — Market (Weeks 13-15): Launch the student-run Eco-Store; host a community recycling event; publish first public impact report.

Phase 6 — Scale (Weeks 16-18): Document and open-source the model; train the next cohort; submit follow-on grant applications.

Safety: All machine operations require certification (video + quiz + supervised demo + signed contract). Ratio: 1 certified adult per 4 students. Ventilation, PPE, and temperature limits are mandatory and audited termly.

Assessment: Students are assessed on NGSS/Common Core/IB standards via products, data reports, and presentations (rubric provided).

docs.text:
Outcome Target (Year 1) Measurement Caps diverted 10,000+ units IR sensor + manual audit Waste diverted 35+ kg Weekly weight logs CO₂e avoided 65+ kg EPA WARM model Students engaged [50-300] Role sign-ups Students certified [25+] Certification log Product revenue $500+ Command Center P&L Products manufactured 200+ units Inventory tracker Community events 2+ Event log Grant follow-ons submitted 1+ Documentation

docs.title: 7. SUSTAINABILITY (150 words)
docs.text: Cap Collective is designed to outlive its grant. Product sales generate ongoing revenue (60-85% margins) that funds consumables and equipment maintenance. The program becomes a permanent, student-managed fixture of the school's STEM curriculum. Documentation is open-source, allowing other schools to replicate at near-zero cost. Over three years, we project self-sufficiency through a combination of product revenue, school budget line items, and reinvestment of savings on waste management.

docs.title: 8. EVALUATION (150 words)
docs.text: We will evaluate success using the metrics in Section 5, reviewed monthly by the Program Lead and termly by leadership. Student learning is assessed against NGSS/Common Core/IB standards using the provided rubric. We will gather qualitative feedback via student surveys and staff reflection. All results are compiled into public impact reports and shared with the funder at [quarterly/annual] intervals.

docs.title: 9. CONCLUSION
docs.text: Cap Collective turns a daily environmental problem into a measurable educational and economic asset. With [grant amount], [School Name] will divert [10,000+] caps, certify [50+] students, and build a self-sustaining program that serves as a regional model. This is not a one-time project — it is infrastructure for a zero-waste campus economy.

docs.title: 1.1 Design Thinking Framework (5 Stages)

3. IDEATE     → Sketch 10+ ideas. No bad ideas yet.
4. PROTOTYPE  → Make it (paper → CAD → physical).
5. TEST       → Does it work? Get feedback. Iterate.

docs.title: 1.3 CAD Tools by Level
docs.text:
Grade Tool Output 3-5 Tinkercad Simple 3D + DXF 6-8 Fusion 360 (basic) 3D parts, molds, DXF 9-12 Fusion 360 (advanced) Complex molds, assemblies

Fusion 360 uses: - Design 2D DXF for laser cutting - Design 3D molds via shape subtraction - Design machine add-ons (e.g., counter housing)

docs.title: 2.1 COASTER (Any tier)
docs.text:
1. COLLECT caps (#2 HDPE — check!)
2. SHRED to 5-8mm flakes (sieve)
3. MELT: parchment sandwich, 140°C, 5 min + flip 5 min
4. COOL under weight
5. DESIGN a DXF in Fusion 360 (circle/square + logo)
6. LASER cut the sheet (low power, high speed)
7. SAND edges (120→400 grit)
8. Done!
Yield: ~120g caps → 1 coaster set (×4)

docs.title: 2.2 DESK ORGANIZER
docs.text:
1-5. Same as coaster (make sheet)
6. DESIGN a fold-up / slot assembly in Fusion 360
7. LASER cut flat-pack parts
8. ASSEMBLE (no glue — friction fit or slot)
9. QC: smooth all edges

docs.title: 2.3 KEYCHAIN (Injection Molder)
docs.text:
1. COLLECT + SHRED
2. DESIGN a two-part mold (gate + vent) in Fusion 360
3. FABRICATE mold: 3D print or CNC mill
4. INJECT: barrel 180°C, clamp mold, pull lever
5. DEMOLD after 2-3 min
6. TRIM flash with cutters
7. Add keyring loop
8. QC

docs.title: 2.4 PLANT POT / SEEDLING TRAY (Injection)
docs.text:
1-2. Collect + shred
3-6. Mold (as above), produce pot
7. Drill drainage hole (if needed)
8. QC: no cracks, even walls

docs.title: 2.5 OUTDOOR TILE (FabLab/Center)
docs.text:
1-5. Collect, shred, melt into a LARGE sheet
6. PRESS into 12×12" frame (larger press)
7. Texturize top (optional stamp)
8. CURE 24 hrs
9. QC: flatness, no cracks

docs.title: 2.6 3D PRINTER FILAMENT (Center)
docs.text:
1-2. Collect + shred
3. DRY flakes (moisture ruins filament)
4. EXTRUDE: feed through filament maker at 1.75mm
5. WIND onto reel at steady speed
6. QC: measure diameter (±0.05mm), test print

docs.title: 3.1 The QC Mindset
docs.text: Every product is a data point. If it fails, we learn. Document everything.

docs.title: 3.2 QC Checklist (Per Batch)
docs.text:
BATCH QC RECORD
Batch #: ______  Date: ______  Operators: ______
Material: ☐ HDPE #2  ☐ PP #5   Color: ______

INCOMING (flakes):
☐ Size uniform (5-8mm sieve) ________
☐ No visible contamination ________
☐ Color consistent (or intentional mix) ________
☐ Dry (no moisture) ________

PRODUCTION (sheet/product):
☐ Thickness ±0.5mm → measured: ____ mm
☐ No burn marks / discoloration ________
☐ No voids/bubbles visible ________
☐ Dimensions match spec: ____ × ____ mm
☐ Edges sanded smooth (no sharp) ________
☐ Branding stamp applied ________

VERDICT: ☐ PASS  ☐ FAIL — reason: ____________
QC Signature: ______________

docs.title: 3.3 Defect Diagnosis Table
docs.text: Defect Root Cause Fix Prevention Voids/bubbles Uneven flake size Re-sieve, pre-mix Standardize shred Warping Fast cooling Cool under weight Weight + slow cool Burn marks Temp too high Lower to 140°C IR thermo checks Discoloration Contaminated caps Reject dirty caps Stricter wash QC Weak/brittle Mixed polymers Sort by #2/#5 only Material ID training Rough edges No sanding Sand 120→400 Finishing SOP Sticking in mold No release agent Apply agent Prep checklist Short shots Underfilled mold More material, hotter Calibrate barrel Flashing Overfilled mold Less material, tighter clamp Clamp torque spec

docs.title: 3.4 Rejection Handling
docs.text:
FAILED BATCH → Re-shred → Re-process → Document lesson → Try again
Nothing is wasted — a failed product is just future feedstock. This is the "infinite loop."

docs.title: 4.1 Cost Per Unit Formula
docs.text:
Material Cost = (grams used / 1000) × cost per kg of input
  → HDPE flake equivalent: assume $0.50/kg (collection is free)
Labor Cost = (minutes × wage rate) — use $0 for student labor, but track hours
Overhead = electricity + consumables + depreciation (estimate $0.10/unit)
Total Cost = Material + Overhead (+ Labor if applicable)

docs.title: 4.2 Pricing Strategy
docs.text:
Price = Total Cost × 3  (gives ~65-70% margin after costs)
OR
Price = Comparable retail price (market-based) if higher

docs.title: 4.4 True Break-Even (Including Equipment)
docs.text:
Equipment investment: $1,000 (Core tier)
Avg margin per unit: ~$9
Break-even units: $1,000 / $9 ≈ 112 units
Realistic: Sell 112 products to pay back equipment. Then profit funds the garden.

docs.title: Our Pledge
docs.text:
We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

docs.title: Positive Behavior
docs.text:
• Empathy & Kindness: Demonstrate empathy and kindness toward other people
  • Respect: Respect differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
  • Constructive Feedback: Give and gracefully accept constructive feedback
  • Accountability: Accept responsibility and apologize to those affected by our mistakes, and learn from the experience
  • Community Focus: Focus on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community
  • Inclusion: Actively welcome and support people of all backgrounds and identities
  • Mentorship: Support newcomers, share knowledge generously, celebrate others' successes

docs.title: Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
• Harassment: Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, personal or political attacks
  • Discrimination: Demeaning comments based on protected characteristics
  • Sexual Harassment: Unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, sexually explicit content
  • Doxxing: Publishing others' private information without explicit permission
  • Threats: Physical threats, violence, intimidation, stalking
  • Spam/Self-Promotion: Off-topic marketing, excessive self-promotion
  • Disruption: Deliberate disruption of discussions, events, or workflows
  • Impersonation: Pretending to be another person or entity
  • Illegal Activity: Encouraging or facilitating illegal acts

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces: - GitHub (issues, PRs, discussions, wiki) - Discord server - Email lists - Social media (when representing Cap Collective) - In-person events (workshops, conferences, meetups) - Virtual events (webinars, office hours, hackathons) - Any other spaces managed by the Cap Collective community

It also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Report violations to: conduct@capcollective.org

Include: - Your contact info (can be anonymous) - Description of incident (what, when, where) - People involved - Any evidence (screenshots, logs, links) - Desired outcome (if any)

All reports are confidential. We will not reveal reporter identity without explicit consent.

docs.title: Response Process
docs.text:
1. Acknowledgment within 24 hours
  2. Investigation by Code of Conduct Committee (3 members)
  3. Decision within 7 days (or communicated timeline)
  4. Action implemented
  5. Follow-up with reporter

docs.title: Enforcement Guidelines
docs.text:
Severity Behavior Consequence 1. Correction Inappropriate language, minor disruption Private written warning, public apology if public 2. Warning Repeated minor, single moderate (insults, mild harassment) Temporary ban (7-30 days), public if public 3. Temporary Ban Severe harassment, discrimination, threats 30-90 day ban from all spaces, appeal after 30 days 4. Permanent Ban Severe/repeated violations, doxxing, violence, illegal acts Permanent ban from all spaces, no appeal

Factors considered: Impact (not intent), pattern, power dynamics, vulnerability of target, community safety.

docs.title: Reporting a Vulnerability
docs.text: DO NOT open a public GitHub issue for security vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Report Privately
docs.text:
Email: security@capcollective.org

Include: - Description of the vulnerability - Steps to reproduce (if possible) - Affected components (dashboard, firmware, docs, etc.) - Potential impact assessment - Suggested fix (if known) - Your contact information for follow-up

docs.title: Response Timeline
docs.text: Phase Target Acknowledgment 24 hours Initial Assessment 72 hours Fix Development 7-30 days (based on severity) Release/Disclosure Coordinated with reporter

docs.title: Severity Classification
docs.text: Level Criteria Response Target Critical RCE, auth bypass, data breach, safety risk 24-48 hours High Auth bypass, privilege escalation, major data leak 1 week Medium XSS, CSRF, info disclosure, DoS 2-4 weeks Low Minor info leak, minor config issue Next release

docs.title: Coordinated Disclosure
docs.text:
1. Reporter submits vulnerability privately
  2. Team acknowledges within 24 hours
  3. Team validates and assesses severity
  4. Team develops fix + tests
  5. Team coordinates release date with reporter
  6. Public disclosure after fix is deployed
  7. Credit given to reporter (if desired)

docs.title: Public Disclosure
docs.text:
• Security advisories published on GitHub Security Advisories
  • CVE requested for significant vulnerabilities
  • Blog post for critical/high severity
  • Changelog updated with security fixes

docs.title: No Surprise Releases
docs.text: We will not disclose vulnerabilities before a fix is available, except in cases of active exploitation where immediate mitigation is necessary.

docs.text:

  • Implement mitigations

docs.title: 4. Eradication (4-24 hours)
docs.text:

  • Remove threat actors
  • Patch vulnerabilities
  • Verify clean state

docs.title: 5. Recovery (24-72 hours)
docs.text:
• Restore from clean backups
  • Validate integrity
  • Monitor for recurrence
  • Gradual traffic restoration

docs.title: 6. Post-Incident (1-2 weeks)
docs.text:

  • Action items with owners
  • Documentation updates
  • Process improvements
  • Customer communication (if needed)

docs.title: Before Submitting PR
docs.text:
• No secrets, keys, tokens in code
  • No hardcoded IPs, passwords, URLs
  • Input validation on all user inputs
  • Parameterized queries (no SQL injection)
  • XSS prevention (escape output, CSP)
  • CSRF protection (SameSite cookies, tokens)
  • Proper error handling (no stack traces to user)
  • Logging: no PII, no secrets
  • Dependencies: latest, no critical CVEs
  • Tests: security-relevant paths covered

docs.title: Everything Needed to Safely Certify a Student Operator
docs.text: The kit references "10-question quiz" and "certification cards" — here they are, fully written.

docs.title: PART 1: TRAINING PATH (Recap & Detail)
docs.text:
MODULE 0: Orientation (all)        20 min
MODULE 1: General Safety (all)     30 min
MODULE 2: Material ID (all)        20 min
MODULE 3: Machine-Specific (per)   30 min each
MODULE 4: Supervised Practice       30 min per machine
ASSESSMENT: Quiz (80%) + Practical
AWARD: Certification Card

Trainer: Certified staff. Ratio: 1 trainer : 6 students max.

docs.title: PART 2: MODULE SCRIPTS (For the Trainer to Deliver)
MODULE 0 — ORIENTATION (20 min)
docs.text: Objectives: Understand what the program does; know the 5 steps; know the rules exist for a reason. Deliver: 1. Why caps matter (3 min) — the marine debris story. 2. The 5 steps (5 min) — Collect → Clean → Shred → Melt → Refine. 3. Tour of stations (7 min) — point out each machine, PPE location, extinguisher, first aid, exits. 4. The rules (5 min) — no cert = no machine; PPE always; never exceed 200°C; report everything. Check: Each student can name the 5 steps and locate the extinguisher.

docs.title: MODULE 1 — GENERAL SAFETY (30 min)
docs.text: Objectives: Identify hazards; don correct PPE; know emergency procedures. Deliver: 1. PPE fitting (10 min) — goggles, gloves, respirator, apron (fit check each student). 2. Hazards walk (10 min) — point out hot surfaces, blades, cables, water/electrical separation. 3. Emergency drill (10 min) — fire, burn, cut, fume. Practice "Stop, Tell, Help." Check: Student states the response to a burn and where the fire blanket is.

docs.title: MODULE 2 — MATERIAL IDENTIFICATION (20 min)
docs.text: Objectives: Distinguish HDPE (#2) and PP (#5) from PET (#1) and PVC (#3); remove liners. Deliver: 1. Show real caps and the number-in-triangle symbol. 2. Sorting drill — mix caps, students sort into HDPE / PP / reject. 3. Liner removal demo — the silicone/foam inner seal. 4. Why it matters — mixed polymer = weak product; PVC = toxic gas. Check: Student sorts 10 caps correctly (≥9/10).

docs.title: MODULE 3 — MACHINE-SPECIFIC (30 min each)
docs.text: Deliver per machine following its SOP (Safety file Section 2): - Heat Press (Grade 6+, Red card) - Shredder (Grade 6+, Orange card) - Laser (Grade 8+, Green card) - Injection Molder (Grade 9+, Blue card) - Saws/Sander (Grade 9+, Purple card)

docs.title: MODULE 4 — SUPERVISED PRACTICE (30 min per machine)
docs.text: Student performs the full operation twice under supervision; trainer signs off on each step.

docs.title: QUIZ A — GENERAL SAFETY (Required for all cards)
docs.text:
Name: __________________ Date: ______ Grade: ____ Pass mark: 8/10

1. What is the ABSOLUTE maximum temperature any machine may reach? a) 140°C b) 180°C c) 200°C d) 260°C

2. Which PPE is required at the heat press? (circle all) Goggles / Heat gloves / VOC respirator / Apron / Ear protection

3. True or False: You may operate a machine if a friend supervises you.

4. What do you do FIRST if you smell burning plastic?

5. Which plastic is NEVER allowed (releases toxic gas)? a) HDPE #2 b) PP #5 c) PVC #3 d) LDPE #4

6. Why must silicone/foam liners be removed from caps?

7. If a cap touches the hot metal platen, what could happen?

8. List the 5 steps of the process in order: 1) ______ 2) ______ 3) ______ 4) ______ 5) ______

9. Where is the fire extinguisher / fire blanket located?

10. True or False: You should report a near-miss even if no one was hurt.

Quiz A Answer Key: 1-c; 2-all four (goggles, gloves, respirator, apron — not ear pro); 3-False; 4-Shut off machine / evacuate / ventilate / tell adult; 5-c; 6-They don't melt and ruin the product/contaminate it; 7-It burns/scorches, discolors and weakens the product; 8-Collect, Clean, Shred, Melt, Refine; 9-[school-specific]; 10-True.

docs.title: QUIZ B — HEAT PRESS (Red card)
docs.text:
Pass mark: 8/10

1. Correct temperature for HDPE? ____ For PP? ____ 2. What goes between the flakes and the metal platen? a) nothing b) parchment paper c) aluminum foil d) cloth 3. How long do you press before flipping? ____ 4. True/False: You may leave the press unattended while pressing. 5. What is "thermal runaway" and what do you do?

6. How do you verify the platen is at temperature? ______________ 7. Why cool the sheet "under weight"? ______________ 8. What PPE is mandatory? ______________ 9. Target sheet thickness tolerance? ______ 10. What do you do with a failed (burned) sheet? ______________

Answer Key B: 1-140°C / 170°C; 2-b; 3-5 min; 4-False; 5-Temp keeps rising beyond set point — cut power at wall, evacuate, report; 6-IR thermometer; 7-Prevent warping; 8-Goggles, heat gloves, respirator, apron; 9-±0.5mm; 10-Re-shred and reuse (never bin the plastic).

docs.title: QUIZ C — SHREDDER (Orange card)
docs.text:
Pass mark: 8/10

1. How do you push material into the shredder? ______ 2. How fast do you feed caps? ______ 3. What do you do if the motor stalls? ______ 4. Target flake size? ______ 5. True/False: You may reach into the hopper to clear a jam while it's running. 6. What PPE is required? ______ 7. What is the e-stop and where is it? ______ 8. Why sieve the flakes? ______ 9. What maintenance happens after each session? ______ 10. Who may operate the shredder? ______

Answer Key C: 1-With the plunger tool, never hands; 2-Slowly, a few at a time; 3-Stop, reverse, clear, restart; 4-5-8mm; 5-False; 6-Goggles, ear protection, apron; 7-Emergency stop button — [location]; 8-Consistent size = better melt; 9-Oil the blades; 10-Only certified operators (Orange card, Grade 6+).

docs.title: QUIZ D — LASER (Green card) — abbreviated
docs.text:
1. Focus the beam on the ____ of the material. (surface)
  2. For recycled plastic use ____ power and ____ speed. (low / high)
  3. Ventilation must be ____ while cutting. (on)
  4. Never cut ____ plastic (releases chlorine gas). (PVC)
  5. True/False: You may leave the laser cutting and walk away. (False)
  6. Keep a ____ within reach at all times. (fire extinguisher)
  7. If the material ignites, ____ (pause/stop, don't open lid immediately, follow fire SOP).
  8. Minimum grade for laser certification? (Grade 8)
  9. What do you do before cutting a new material? (confirm it's approved plastic)
  10. Where do you record the cut? (Command Center batch log)

docs.title: QUIZ E — INJECTION MOLDER (Blue card) — abbreviated
docs.text:
1. Barrel temperature for HDPE. (~180°C)
  2. What secures the mold under the nozzle? (C-clamp, tight)
  3. How long to wait before demolding? (2-3 min)
  4. How is plastic injected? (steady firm lever pressure until stop)
  5. What is the gate / vent for? (plastic entry / air escape)
  6. Why apply release agent? (so product doesn't stick)
  7. Minimum grade? (Grade 9)
  8. What PPE? (goggles, heat gloves, respirator, apron)
  9. Never touch the ____. (barrel/nozzle)
  10. Failed part → ? (re-shred, mono-material)

docs.title: QUIZ F — SAW / SANDER (Purple card) — abbreviated
docs.text:
1. Keep fingers at least ____ from the blade. (5 cm)
  2. Feed material ____ the blade rotation. (against)
  3. Tie back ____; remove ____. (hair / jewelry)
  4. Clamp the work — True/False? (True — always clamp)
  5. Where does dust go? (extraction/capture)
  6. PPE? (goggles, ear protection, apron, dust mask)
  7. What before changing a blade? (disconnect power)
  8. Never reach ____ a moving blade. (across)
  9. Minimum grade? (Grade 9)
  10. After use: (wait for full stop, clear dust)

docs.title: 12 Full, Teachable Lesson Plans (3 per Grade Band)
docs.text:
Each plan includes objectives, standards, materials, timed procedure, differentiation, assessment & extension.

Pairs with 06_CURRICULUM_STANDARDS_MAPPING.md. Adapt timings to your period length.

docs.title: LESSON K1: What Are Plastic Caps? (45 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students classify caps by observable properties and identify that caps differ from bottles. Standards: K-ESS3-3, 2-PS1-1 Materials: Pile of mixed caps, magnifiers, sorting mats, worksheet K1 Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-5 | Hook: Hold up a bottle and a cap. "Are these the same?" | | 5-15 | Explore: Students handle caps — feel, look, smell (clean ones only) | | 15-30 | Sort: By color, then by size, then by "bumpy/smooth" | | 30-40 | Share: Each group explains ONE way they sorted | | 40-45 | Wrap: "Caps and bottles are different. That's why we keep caps separate." | Differentiation: EAL — picture cards; advanced — sort by 3 attributes. Assessment: Sorting worksheet K1 (correct classification). Extension: Count a cup of caps; graph as a class.

docs.title: LESSON K2: Cap's Journey (45 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students sequence where a cap can go and explain why recycling is better. Standards: K-ESS3-3 Materials: "Cap's Journey" story, sequence cards, glue Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-10 | Read "Cap's Journey" aloud (Printable Resources) | | 10-25 | Sequence cards: bottle → bin → (ocean OR box → coaster) | | 25-35 | Act it out — students play roles | | 35-45 | Discuss: "Which path is better? Why?" | Assessment: Correctly sequence 5 cards. Extension: Draw your own "good journey" for a cap.

docs.title: LESSON K3: Count & Graph (45 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students count collected caps and represent data in a bar graph. Standards: K.CC.B.4, 1.MD.C.4, 2.MD.D.10 Materials: This week's caps, graphing paper, sticky dots Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-10 | Count caps as a class (every 10th one a different color) | | 10-30 | Build a class bar graph by color | | 30-40 | "Which color won? How many more?" | | 40-45 | Predict next week's total | Assessment: Graph correct; answers comparison questions. Extension: Set a class goal for next week.

docs.title: LESSON E1: Build the Box (90 min, double period)
docs.text: Objective: Students assemble a collection box and explain how it works. Standards: 3-5-ETS1-1, 3.MD.B.4 Materials: cad/collection_box.scad cut parts, glue, clamps, acrylic, screws Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-10 | Show CAD design; explain finger/screw joints | | 10-20 | Measure and check all parts present | | 20-70 | Assemble: glue edges, clamp, screw, set 60s per joint | | 70-85 | Install acrylic window; test drop slot | | 85-90 | Reflect: "What would you change about the design?" | Differentiation: Roles — measurer, gluer, clamp-holder, checker. Assessment: Box is square, flush, functional; design reflection. Extension: Design a sign for the box.

docs.title: LESSON E2: From Caps to Coaster (90 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students trace the melt process and design a coaster in Tinkercad. Standards: 3-5-ETS1-1/2, 5-PS1-3 Materials: Pre-made flakes, heat press (teacher demo), Tinkercad, worksheet E2 Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-15 | Safety briefing + watch teacher run a press cycle | | 15-30 | Measure flakes (weight), predict sheet thickness | | 30-70 | Design a coaster in Tinkercad (circle + pattern) | | 70-85 | Export DXF; compare designs | | 85-90 | Reflect: "How did the plastic change? Why?" | Assessment: Design file exported; states states-of-matter change. Extension: Design a matching keychain.

docs.title: LESSON E3: The Numbers (45 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students calculate yield and graph collection data. Standards: 5-PS1-3, 5.MD.A.1, 5.NF.B.3 Materials: Scale, calc sheets, graph paper Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-10 | Weigh flakes; record grams | | 10-25 | Calculate yield: grams of product ÷ grams of flakes | | 25-40 | Graph weekly collection counts | | 40-45 | Discuss: "What affects yield?" | Assessment: Correct yield %; graph accurate. Extension: Predict weight of a full box.

docs.title: LESSON I1: Programming the Counter (90 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students wire and program an IR beam-break counter. Standards: MS-ETS1-2, MS-PS4-2 Materials: ESP32, IR sensor, jumper wires, laptop, Arduino IDE, sensor_count.ino Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-15 | Explain beam-break sensing; show wiring diagram | | 15-40 | Wire ESP32 + sensor; verify with serial monitor | | 40-70 | Upload code; test with falling caps; adjust debounce | | 70-85 | Troubleshoot miscounts; document | | 85-90 | Reflect: "What causes false counts? How did you fix it?" | Differentiation: Pair stronger coders with beginners; provide filled-in code as scaffold. Assessment: Working counter; documentation of fix. Extension: Add fill-level alert at 90%.

docs.title: LESSON I2: Life Cycle Assessment (90 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students compare environmental impact of recycled vs virgin HDPE. Standards: MS-PS1-3, MS-LS2-5 Materials: Research links, worksheet I2, Command Center Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-15 | Define LCA stages: raw → production → use → disposal | | 15-45 | Research: energy & CO₂ for virgin vs recycled HDPE | | 45-75 | Build comparison table; calculate our CO₂e avoided | | 75-90 | Present findings; debate: "Is recycling worth it?" | Assessment: Accurate data; evidence-based argument. Extension: LCA for PP or aluminum.

docs.text: Objective: Students cost a product and set a price to make a profit. Standards: MS-ETS1-2, 7.RP.A.1, 6.RP.A.1 Materials: Calculator, worksheet I3, cost data Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-15 | Explain cost components (material, overhead, labor) | | 15-45 | Cost 2 products using the formula | | 45-70 | Set price (cost ×3); calculate margin; compare to retail | | 70-90 | "Investor pitch" — 2 min per team to a panel | Assessment: Correct costing; persuasive pitch. docs.title: LESSON S1: Polymer Science & Rheology (90 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students measure how HDPE flows and shrinks, and explain processing implications. Standards: HS-PS2-6, HS-PS1-3 Materials: Flakes, press, calipers, IR thermo, worksheet S1 Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-20 | Polymer basics: chains, amorphous vs crystalline, Tg/Tm | | 20-50 | Experiment: melt at 130/140/150°C; measure flow & surface | | 50-70 | Measure shrinkage after cooling; calculate % | | 70-90 | Analyze: what processing temp gives best result? Why? | Assessment: Data table; justified conclusion. Extension: Test PP (higher Tm) and compare.

docs.title: LESSON S2: Systems Optimization (90 min)
docs.text: Objective: Students map the full workflow, identify a bottleneck, and propose a data-backed fix. Standards: HS-ETS1-3, HSS.ID.B.6 Materials: Command Center data, timer, worksheet S2 Procedure: | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-20 | Map the process (flowchart) with cycle times | | 20-45 | Collect timing data for each step (hands-on) | | 45-70 | Find the bottleneck; propose a fix; predict impact | | 70-90 | Present & critique proposals | Assessment: Correct bottleneck ID; quantified improvement. Extension: Implement and re-measure (A/B).

docs.title: LESSON S3: Grant Writing & Scale (2 periods)
docs.text: Objective: Students write a real grant application to fund expansion. Standards: W.9-10.1, HS-ETS1-3 Materials: 08_GRANT_... templates, Command Center impact data Procedure (P1): | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-15 | Analyze a real grant call; identify criteria | | 15-45 | Draft need + approach sections | | 45-90 | Draft outcomes + budget (use our real data) | Procedure (P2): | Min | Activity | |-----|----------| | 0-30 | Finish + peer review against rubric | | 30-70 | Present to a "board" (staff panel) | | 70-90 | Revise and submit best application for real | Assessment: Complete application; meets funder criteria. docs.text: "Cap Collective is a student-run program that turns bottle cap waste into sellable products. It teaches STEM, entrepreneurship, and sustainability, generates revenue for the school, and gives us grant-worthy measurable impact. We can pilot it for under $1,000."

8 Tabs | Auto-calculating | Chart-ready | Grant-report-ready

How to build it: Create a new Google Sheet named "Cap Collective Command Center". Create 8 tabs with the exact names below, paste the headers and starting formulas, then duplicate rows as needed. Importable CSV files for each tab are in the csv/ folder of this kit.

docs.title: Webhook Setup (Google Apps Script)
docs.text:
function doPost(e) {
  var sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActiveSpreadsheet().getSheetByName("Sensor Data Log");
  var data = JSON.parse(e.postData.contents);
  sheet.appendRow([
    new Date(), data.binId, data.count, data.fill,
    data.temp, "OK", "ESP32"
  ]);
  return ContentService.createTextOutput("OK");
}

docs.title: SCRIPT A — LAUNCH ASSEMBLY (5-7 min)
docs.text:
(Two students + Program Lead on stage. Cap in a jar as a prop.)

[Student 1]: "Good morning everyone. How many of you drank something from a plastic bottle this week?" (hands) "That's a LOT. Here's the thing — the bottle usually gets recycled. But the CAP? Usually not."

[Student 2]: "Only 3 percent of bottle caps get recycled. The rest end up in landfill — or the ocean. Sea turtles and fish eat them because they look like food."

[Student 1]: "So we're doing something about it. Starting today, bottle caps have a new job at this school."

[Program Lead]: "Introducing Cap Collective. [X] collection boxes are now around campus. Every cap you drop in gets counted, washed, and turned into something new — coasters, organizers, plant pots. And the money funds our garden."

[Student 2]: "Here's how you can help: 1 — find a cap. 2 — drop it in a box. 3 — watch our live count go up."

[Student 1]: "We even have a machine that counts every cap automatically. You can see the number live on the screen right now." (show dashboard)

[Program Lead]: "This Friday is our first Collection Day. The class with the most caps wins [prize]. Let's build the bridge. Join the Bridge. Create the Impact." (applause)

docs.title: SCRIPT B — PA ANNOUNCEMENTS (30 sec each)
docs.text:
PA-1 (Monday):

"Good morning! Cap Collective launches today. Look for the big wooden boxes — drop your bottle caps in. Every cap counts. Let's go!"

PA-2 (Friday):

"It's the FIRST Cap Drop Day! Bring your caps from home and school. The winning class gets [prize]. Drop. Count. Repeat!"

PA-3 (Weekly recurring):

"Cap Collective update: we've collected [X] caps — that's [Y] kilos kept out of landfill. Keep it up!"

PA-4 (Store launch):

"Our Eco-Store is open! Student-made coasters, keychains, and organizers — made from YOUR caps. Find us at [location]."

docs.title: SCRIPT C — FIRST CAP DROP CEREMONY (Friday, 10 min)
docs.text:
1. Program Lead welcomes everyone to the main box.
2. A student leader holds up the "Golden Cap" (spray-painted cap).
3. Principal drops the GOLDEN CAP into the box first — the symbolic first cap.
4. Students cheer; sensor counts it; projector shows the number = 1.
5. Each class rep drops a handful.
6. Announce the competition + prize.
7. Group photo for comms.

docs.title: PRESS RELEASE TEMPLATE
docs.text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
[Date]

STUDENTS TURN BOTTLE CAPS INTO PRODUCTS AT [SCHOOL]
New Student-Led Program Diverts Plastic Waste and Funds the Garden

[City, Date] — [School Name] today launched Cap Collective, a
student-run program that collects bottle caps and transforms them
into sellable products such as coasters, organizers, and plant pots.

Only about 3% of bottle caps are recycled globally, and because of
their small size they often escape industrial sorting and end up in
landfills or oceans. Cap Collective captures caps at the source,
using a five-step process: collect, clean, shred, melt, and refine.

"Students aren't just learning about sustainability — they're building
it," said [Program Lead]. "Every cap they drop in becomes a product,
and every product funds our garden."

In its first semester, the program aims to divert more than 10,000
caps (35+ kg), certify [X] students, and generate $500+ in revenue.

[Quote from Principal.]

MEDIA CONTACT: [Name, email, phone]
PHOTO/VIDEO OPPORTUNITIES: [dates/times]

docs.text:

docs.title: 3.5 Cleaning Protocol (CRITICAL)
docs.text:
This is the most important step for quality.

  1. Sort: HDPE #2 vs PP #5 (check underside symbol)
  2. Remove liners: Pull out silicone/foam inner seals (they don't melt!)
  3. Soak: Warm water + dish soap, 10 min
  4. Scrub: Old toothbrush for stubborn residue
  5. Rinse: Until water runs clear
  6. Dry: Air dry 24 hours on mesh (no towel — lint!)
  7. QC: Any cap with adhesive/paper/liquid smell → reject

Why: Residual milk/sugar burns at high temp → toxic fumes + discolored product.

docs.title: 3.6 Shredding SOP (Grade 6+, Certified)
docs.text:
1. Clear blades of residual plastic
  2. Toggle motor, verify rotation
  3. Feed slowly — do not overfeed (stalls motor)
  4. Target flake size: 5-8mm
  5. Sieve through mesh screen (consistency)
  6. Store in labeled buckets by color
  7. Oil blades after each session

docs.title: 3.7 Heat Press SOP (Grade 6+, Certified)
docs.text:
HDPE Settings: 140°C | PP Settings: 170°C

  1. Turn on press, set temp & time
  2. Wait for platen to reach FULL temp (verify with IR thermometer)
  3. Parchment sandwich: flakes between two baking-paper sheets
  4. Press 5 min → flip → press 5 min
  5. Cool under weight (prevents warping)
  6. Remove, measure thickness

⚠️ WARNING: Never let plastic touch the metal platen. Monitor constantly — thermal runaway is possible.

docs.title: What Is Cap Collective?
docs.text:
Cap Collective is a student-led circular recycling program that captures discarded plastic bottle caps and transforms them into useful products — while funding the school garden. Students run every part of it: collection, cleaning, shredding, melting, product design, sales, and impact reporting.

Bottle caps are a recycling blind spot. Mechanical recycling centers process large items like bottles, but caps are too small — they fall through sorting screens or jam high-speed equipment. The result: a perfectly good, high-grade plastic is thrown away, every day, in every school.

Cap Collective captures that resource at the source and turns it into value.

docs.title: The Problem in One Line
docs.text: Only about 3% of bottle caps are recycled globally. The rest end up in landfill or the ocean — where they look like food to sea turtles and fish.

docs.title: The Solution: A 5-Step Micro-Factory in Your School
docs.text:
1. COLLECT   →  HDPE (#2) & PP (#5) caps dropped in campus boxes
2. CLEAN     →  Remove liners · wash · air-dry 24 hours
3. SHRED     →  Uniform 5-8 mm flakes
4. MELT      →  Heat press: HDPE 140°C · PP 170°C  (never above 200°C)
5. REFINE    →  Laser-cut · injection-mold · press into finished goods

Closed loop: When a product breaks, it goes right back to Step 3. 100% recyclable, forever.

docs.title: Why Caps?
docs.text:
Property Why It Matters HDPE (#2) & PP (#5) Melt predictably; safe when heated carefully High density & color Strong products with beautiful marbled finishes Abundant Every school produces thousands per term Food-safe grade Suitable for useful everyday items Ignored by industry An untapped resource, not a nuisance

No PVC (#3) is ever used — it releases toxic gas when heated.

docs.title: What Students Make
docs.text:
Coasters · keychains · phone stands · desk organizers · plant pots · art tiles · and more.

Each product uses a known number of caps (e.g., a keychain ≈ 4 caps, a coaster ≈ 15 caps), so students can see — and calculate — exactly how waste becomes value.

A live dashboard counts caps automatically (via an optional sensor) and shows the impact in real time.

  3. Never exceed 200°C on any heating device.
  4. Ventilation always on before heating any plastic.
  5. PPE at all times at machine stations.
  6. Stop work immediately if you smell burning, see smoke, or hear grinding.
  7. Hands stay out of shredder hopper and press platen at all times.

docs.title: 1.3 Emergency Procedures
docs.text: FIRE: Activate fire blanket/CO₂ extinguisher. Do NOT use water on plastic fires. Evacuate. Call emergency services. BURN: Cool with running water 10+ min. Do not pop blisters. Report to first aider. CUT: Apply pressure, elevate, seek first aid. Deep cuts → emergency services. FUME/HEADACHE: Turn off machine, evacuate room, ventilate 15 min, report. FULL COLLECTION BOX: Safe — swap box, do not compress.

docs.text: Every incident (near-miss or actual) logged within 24 hours using the form in Appendix. Program Lead reviews weekly.

docs.title: 2.1 HEAT PRESS SOP
docs.text:
▛▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▜
▌  HEAT PRESS — OPERATOR PROCEDURE                    ▐
▟▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▟
BEFORE (each session): 1. Confirm ventilation is ON (feel airflow, check fan running) 2. Don goggles, gloves, respirator, apron 3. Check cord, plug, no damage 4. Verify IR thermometer reads room temp

STARTUP: 1. Press red I/O button (ON) 2. Press SET → set temperature (HDPE 140°C / PP 170°C) 3. Press SET → set time (5:00) 4. Wait for FULL temp — verify with IR thermometer

OPERATION: 1. Place parchment sheet on platen 2. Arrange flakes (evenly, ~equal coverage) 3. Cover with second parchment sheet 4. Lower platen (do not touch hot surface) 5. Maintain pressure 5 minutes 6. Release, flip the "sandwich", press 5 minutes again 7. Cool under weight 5 minutes 8. Remove, inspect

⚠️ DANGER — THERMAL RUNAWAY: If temp exceeds set point and keeps rising → cut power at wall → evacuate → report.

SHUTDOWN: Off → cool 20 min → clean platen with approved cleaner.

Maintenance: Clean platen weekly. Check cable monthly.

docs.title: 2.2 SHREDDER SOP
docs.text:
▛▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▜
▌  SHREDDER — OPERATOR PROCEDURE                      ▐
▟▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▄▟
BEFORE: 1. Don goggles, ear protection, apron 2. Clear blades of residual plastic 3. Check emergency stop button works 4. Verify catch bin is empty

OPERATION: 1. Toggle motor — verify correct rotation 2. Feed slowly — a few caps at a time 3. NEVER use hands to push material — use the plunger 4. If motor stalls → stop → reverse → clear → restart 5. Target flake size: 5-8mm 6. Sieve through mesh screen

⚠️ NEVER: Put hands in hopper, overfeed, run unattended, remove guards.

SHUTDOWN: Run until clear → off → clean → oil blades.

docs.title: 2.3 INJECTION MOLDER SOP (Center tier, 9-12 only)
docs.text: BEFORE: Full PPE. Verify ventilation. Inspect mold. STARTUP: Set barrel to 180°C. Wait for full heat. OPERATION: 1. Load flakes into hopper 2. Wait for molten state 3. Clamp mold tightly (C-clamp) 4. Pull lever — steady, firm pressure until stop 5. Wait 2-3 min for solidification 6. Demold carefully (use pliers) ⚠️ NEVER: Touch barrel. Open mold while hot. Force jammed plunger. SHUTDOWN: Purge barrel. Off. Cool.

docs.title: 2.4 LASER CUTTER SOP (Center tier)
docs.text: BEFORE: Extract ventilation ON. Fire extinguisher within reach. Know material (recycled plastic only — no PVC!). OPERATION: 1. Focus beam on sheet surface 2. Set LOW power / HIGH speed for recycled plastic (prevents flaring) 3. NEVER leave laser unattended while cutting 4. Watch for flame; pause if ignited ⚠️ NEVER: Cut unknown plastics (PVC releases chlorine gas). Run unattended. SHUTDOWN: Off → clean lens → clear debris.

docs.title: 2.5 SANDER / FRET SAW / BANDSAW SOP
docs.text: BEFORE: Goggles, ear pro, apron. Tie back hair. Remove jewelry. OPERATION: Clamp work. Keep fingers 5cm+ from blade. Feed against rotation. Never reach across. SHUTDOWN: Off. Wait for full stop. Clear dust.

docs.title: Keep the Program Alive When People Leave
docs.text: End-of-year close-out, leadership succession, summer maintenance, credentials, and a clean new-year reset.

docs.title: PART 1: WHY THIS MATTERS
docs.text:
Most school programs die when their founder graduates or transfers. This guide makes Cap Collective bigger than any one person.

Golden rule: Assume the lead leaves tomorrow. Would the program survive? If not, fix it now.

docs.title: PART 2: THE LIVING BINDER (Single Source of Truth)
docs.text:
Keep one shared, backed-up location (Drive/SharePoint) containing: 

/Cap Collective
  ├── README (start here)
  ├── All kit docs (00-28)
  ├── /csv  (data)
  ├── /cad  (designs)
  ├── /resources (code)
  ├── /data-archive (past years)
  ├── /photos (with releases)
  ├── /grants (awarded + reports)
  └── PASSWORDS → use a password manager, NOT this folder
Rule: If it's not written down in the binder, it doesn't exist.

docs.title: PART 3: END-OF-YEAR CLOSE-OUT CHECKLIST
docs.text: (Do this in the final 3 weeks of the school year.)

docs.title: Data & Records
docs.text: ☐ Close the year's data; freeze a copy in /data-archive/[year] ☐ Export Command Center tabs to CSV/PDF ☐ Generate the Annual Report (23_...) ☐ Log all certifications; note who expires when ☐ Back up the dashboard and sensor data

docs.title: Physical Assets
docs.text: ☐ Clean and service all machines ☐ Inventory equipment against the asset list (14_...) ☐ Note repairs needed over summer ☐ Store tools/PPE safely; secure the room ☐ Photograph the current setup for next year

docs.title: Financial
docs.text: ☐ Reconcile all accounts ☐ Close the P&L; report net to admin ☐ Note remaining balance and where it's held ☐ File all receipts; scan to Drive

docs.title: People & Knowledge
docs.text: ☐ Succession decided (who leads next year?) ☐ Handover meeting held (see Part 4) ☐ Graduating seniors recorded as alumni mentors ☐ Recognize everyone (awards assembly)

docs.title: PART 4: HANDOVER MEETING AGENDA (2 hours)
docs.text:
1. Program recap — what worked, what didn't (30 min)
2. Walk the Living Binder folder-by-folder (20 min)
3. Live demo: dashboard, sensor, POS, forms (20 min)
4. Open items & risks (15 min)
5. Credentials transfer (15 min)
6. Next-year calendar draft (15 min)
7. Q&A + contacts exchanged (5 min)
Record it. Give the next lead the recording.

docs.title: PART 5: CREDENTIAL & ACCOUNT HANDOVER
docs.text:
Never let accounts die because one person owned them.

Account Owner now Transfer to Notes Program email Use a role mailbox, not personal Google Drive Share with ≥2 staff Dashboard (Looker) Sensor project (Arduino Cloud) Social media Store/POS (Square) School/PTA owned Grant portal logins Bank/boosters Adult custodian only

Checklist for each account: ☐ At least 2 staff have access ☐ Recovery email/phone is a role, not a person ☐ Password in the password manager (not a doc) ☐ Old user removed only after new user confirmed

docs.text:
• Never let the program depend on seniors.
  • Use grade pyramid: seniors → juniors → sophomores → freshmen.
  • Each lead role has a co-lead one grade below.
  • Seniors mentor replacements for one full term.
  • Keep an alumni mentor list (they can advise remotely).

When a beloved lead leaves, give them a light ongoing role: - Remote mentor for 1 term - Guest speaker / judge - Grant advisor - Alumni reference for college apps

docs.title: PART 10: IF THE PROGRAM GOES DORMANT (Recovery Plan)

If it stops (staff loss, budget cut): 1. Don't sell the equipment — store it (this kit's asset list helps). 2. Keep the Living Binder intact. 3. Find one champion willing to restart. 4. Restart at Tier 1 (collect + wash) — low cost, low risk. 5. Re-launch using 19_...; rebuild certification.

A dormant program with good docs restarts easily. A chaotic one doesn't.

docs.title: Cap Collective — District Scale & Replication Guide
Go From One School to a Whole District (Without Breaking)
docs.text: Readiness assessment, hub-and-spoke model, train-the-trainer, shared services, and a 12-month rollout.

docs.title: PART 1: WHEN TO SCALE (Don't Rush)
docs.text:
You're ready to replicate when: ☐ Program has run ≥1 full semester ☐ You have documented, working SOPs (this kit) ☐ You have measured impact (real numbers) ☐ At least 2 staff can run it without you ☐ You have a repeatable launch playbook (19_...)

Do NOT scale if: it depends on one hero teacher, you have no data, or safety is shaky.

docs.title: PART 2: SITE READINESS ASSESSMENT (Per New School)
docs.text:
Score each 0-3 (0=no, 3=yes). Minimum 18/30 to launch.

Criterion Score Committed staff champion /3 Admin support /3 Usable space (ventilated) /3 Budget tier identified /3 Safety officer willing /3 Student interest /3 Parent/community support /3 Links to curriculum /3 Data/tech capacity /3 Continuity plan /3 TOTAL /30

docs.title: PART 3: THE HUB-AND-SPOKE MODEL
docs.text:
One "hub" school owns the expensive/rare equipment; "spoke" schools share it.

                ┌──────────────┐
                │   DISTRICT    │
                └──────┬───────┘
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        │              │              │
   ┌────▼────┐   ┌────▼────┐   ┌────▼────┐
   │  HUB    │◄──│ SPOKE A │──►│ SPOKE B │
   │(shared  │   │(collect)│   │(collect)│
   │ equip)  │   └─────────┘   └─────────┘
   └─────────┘
- Spokes do collection, sorting, washing (cheap, safe). - Hub does melting/pressing/injection (expensive, needs ventilation + certification). - Caps flow to the hub; finished products flow back for sale. - Shared van/runner moves material weekly or bi-weekly.

Benefits: 1 machine set serves 5-10 schools; each spoke needs only ~$500 Tier-1.

docs.title: PART 4: SHARED SERVICES (Centralize These)
docs.text: Service Why centralize Procurement Bulk discounts; one PO Grant writing One grant writer, many sites Dashboard/IT One rollup, shared templates Training Train-the-trainer; one curriculum Insurance Umbrella policy Sales/marketing One brand, one ecosystem Data & reporting Consistent metrics Maintenance One technician

docs.title: PART 5: TRAIN-THE-TRAINER MODEL
docs.text:

docs.title: 31. Train-the-Trainer & Ambassador Program
docs.text: Purpose: Make the program self-sustaining by certifying students who certify others and by turning your top students into public ambassadors.

docs.title: 1. Why Train-the-Trainer?
docs.text:
A program that only runs when the founder teacher is present dies at graduation. Building a trainer tier gives you:

Benefit Result Certified senior students Machines run during club hours without the teacher Student trainers Other students learn faster from peers Handover pipeline Autonomous operation by the next cohort

docs.title: 2. The Trainer Tier (green +)
docs.text:
Eligibility:

  • 2 semesters in the program OR 50+ verified logged working hours.
  • Foundation Safety Certificate (doc 17 / try the quiz at learn.html).
  • Pass a practical cascade: the student runs a full batch (collect → clean → shred → melt → refine) with the teacher signing off an observation checklist.

docs.title: Trainer Duties
docs.text:
• Supervise one machine station during club hours.
  • Onboard & observe new card candidates.
  • Update the Command Center sheets (doc 03).
  • Report near-misses immediately to the staff sponsor.

docs.title: Trainer Limits
docs.text:
• A trainer cannot clear a fault alone — a staff member is called for any jam, smoke, or alarm.
  • Trainers train only on their own certified machine card(s).

docs.title: 3. Ambassador Program (outward-facing)
docs.text:
Ambassadors speak and demo for the school community. Roles:

  1. Storyteller — runs the Instagram/photo diary and the impact gallery page.
  2. Demo Captain — hosts launch-week stalls and open days.
  3. Partner Liaison — maintains the supplier directory (doc 30) contacts.
  4. Eco-Store Manager — runs inventory + client checkouts (doc 21).

docs.title: Ambassador Principles
docs.text:
• Script first, ad-lib second: use the launch-deck speaking notes (doc 11).
  • No safety shortcuts in demos: observers get a verbal mini-safety brief before hands-on.
  • One adult present at every public event.

docs.text:

  • Certs are printed from the quiz page or the paper forms (doc 17).
  • Review the roster each term for expiring cards (retest if > 12 months).

docs.title: 5. Measuring Success
docs.text:
Track over the year:

  • Number of student trainers active.
  • Number of certifications issued by trainers (not staff).
  • Ambassador-led events and visits.
  • % of club operations run without staff in the room (target 40% by end of year 2).

// pages or app component
export async function getImpact() {
  const url = "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/XXXX/pub?gid=YYYY&single=true&output=csv";
  const res = await fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" });
  const text = await res.text();
  const [header, ...rows] = text.trim().split("\n");
  // parse rows into metrics
  return rows.map(r => r.split(","));
}
Replace XXXX/YYYY with your sheet ID and tab gid (visible in the URL).

docs.title: 29. IoT & Live Tracking — Auto-Counted Caps
docs.text: Purpose: Replace hand-counting with sensor-based, real-time collection data. Every drop = an automatic log, refreshed every minute.

docs.title: 1. Why Automate?
docs.text:
Problem Manual counting IoT counting Count accuracy ~90% (human fatigue) ~99%+ (weight-based) Time per bag 5–10 minutes 0 (automatic) Motivation Leaderboard updates weekly Leaderboard updates live Teacher overhead High Near zero

The tracker feeds the public dashboard (CAPBOT + website), the class leaderboards, and the semester forecast.

docs.title: 2. Reference Build: Weight-Sensing Hopper (IR-free option)
docs.text:
A load cell under a collection hopper is the most robust school-priced design.

  • Parts (≈ $60–90 per hopper):
  • Load cell 5 kg + HX711 amplifier
  • Arduino Uno / Wemos D1 Mini (Wi-Fi)
  • Available in cad/ and firmware in resources/sensor_count.ino
  • Math: 1 cap ≈ 2.5 g → sensor reading ÷ 0.0025 kg = estimated caps. Recalibrate monthly with a 100-cap test bag.
  • Logic:
  • Weigh hopper every 2 seconds, take a rolling median (3 readings) to cancel vibration noise.
  • When weight increases by ≥ 25 g (≈ 10 caps), the delta is added to the "pending" total.
  • Every 60 seconds, POST the pending total to the tracker API and reset pending to 0.
  • After each POST, record the new baseline weight.

Caps are counted on the way in, so emptying the hopper doesn't double-count.

docs.title: 3. Wiring Into the Live Tracker
docs.text:
POST to the same endpoint the website uses:

POST /api/tracker
{ "school": "AISB", "classLabel": "HOPPER-1", "caps": 240, "date": "YYYY-MM-DD" }

Class leaderboards update automatically. Optionally raise the class label

HOPPER-1-KG

to track hardware reliability per unit.

docs.title: 4. Verification Checklist (before going live)
docs.text:
• Sensor agrees with a manual 100-cap count within ±2%.
  • Hopper handles a full 5 kg bag without jamming or tilting.
  • Wi-Fi reconnects after a power cut (add a watchdog reset).
  • Duplicate POST protection: the board keeps a timestamp of its last successful send.
  • Power: use a 9 V/2 A adapter; add a battery at the school end to survive outages.

docs.title: 5. Data Ethics & Privacy
docs.text:
• Log no student names — only school, class label, caps, timestamp.
  • Onboarding doc (doc 15) must mention the sensor in the permission forms.
  • Data is the school's own; the dashboard is public but aggregate-only, never per-student.

docs.title: 6. Scale-Up Path
docs.text:
1. Semester 1: one hopper in the main hub; website + leaderboard feeds from manual logs too.
  2. Semester 2: hopper per wing/gateway; classes race live.
  3. Year 2 (multi-school): hoppers at partner schools, central dashboard in the Command Center.

-- Cap Collective Supabase Schema
-- ============================================================
-- Run this in Supabase SQL Editor to set up the database
-- Compatible with PostgreSQL 15+ (Supabase default)

-- ============================================================
-- TABLE: cap_counts
-- Stores individual cap count events from IoT sensors
-- ============================================================
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cap_counts (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    node_id SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (node_id BETWEEN 1 AND 10),
    cap_count INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (cap_count > 0),
    cap_color VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (cap_color IN ('red', 'blue', 'green', 'white', 'unknown')),

    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ language 'plpgsql';

-- Apply updated_at triggers

CREATE TRIGGER update_equipment_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON equipment FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION update_updated_at_column();

-- Function to aggregate daily impact metrics
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION refresh_daily_impact_metrics(target_date DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE)
RETURNS VOID AS $$
DECLARE
    v_caps BIGINT;
    v_weight DECIMAL(10,3);
    v_products_made INTEGER;
    v_products_sold INTEGER;
    v_revenue DECIMAL(12,2);
    v_students_engaged INTEGER;
    v_students_certified INTEGER;
    v_co2e DECIMAL(10,2);
BEGIN
    -- Aggregate from collection_events
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(cap_count), 0), COALESCE(SUM(weight_kg), 0)
    INTO v_caps, v_weight
    FROM collection_events
    WHERE collection_date = target_date;

    -- Aggregate from product_batches
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(quantity_made), 0)
    INTO v_products_made
    FROM product_batches
    WHERE production_date = target_date;

    -- Aggregate from sales
    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(quantity), 0), COALESCE(SUM(total_usd), 0)
    INTO v_products_sold, v_revenue
    FROM sales
    WHERE sale_date::DATE = target_date;

    -- Students
    SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE safety_certified OR shredder_certified OR press_certified OR laser_certified)
    INTO v_students_engaged, v_students_certified
    FROM students
    WHERE active = TRUE;

    -- CO2e (EPA WARM model: ~1.9 kg CO2e per kg HDPE)
    v_co2e := v_weight * 1.9;

    -- Upsert
    INSERT INTO impact_metrics (metric_date, caps_collected, weight_kg, products_made, products_sold, revenue_usd, students_engaged, students_certified, co2e_avoided_kg)
    VALUES (target_date, v_caps, v_weight, v_products_made, v_products_sold, v_revenue, v_students_engaged, v_students_certified, v_co2e)
    ON CONFLICT (metric_date) DO UPDATE SET
        caps_collected = EXCLUDED.caps_collected,
        weight_kg = EXCLUDED.weight_kg,
        products_made = EXCLUDED.products_made,
        products_sold = EXCLUDED.products_sold,
        revenue_usd = EXCLUDED.revenue_usd,
        students_engaged = EXCLUDED.students_engaged,
        students_certified = EXCLUDED.students_certified,
        co2e_avoided_kg = EXCLUDED.co2e_avoided_kg,
        updated_at = NOW();
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
